accuracy.evidence: Checked against CCSS ELA RI.4.6 ('Compare and contrast a firsthand and secondhand account of the same event or topic; describe the differences in focus and the information provided') and the DfE 2013 English programme of study for Years 5–6 (distinguish between statements of fact and opinion; make comparisons within and across books). Source types follow the standard definitions: diary, letter, logbook, autobiography and eyewitness interview are firsthand; biography, textbook, encyclopedia and a report built from interviews are secondhand. The flood, the town and Mia are an invented, clearly framed example (diary 2004, history book 2024), so no historical claim can be wrong; the one real event in the challenge (Moon landing TV audience) is used only to say that viewer numbers come from records, not from an astronaut.

misconceptions.evidence: Each documented Grade 4 slip has a target: biography = firsthand because it is about one person (step 1 prediction, challenge tag 'bio'), autobiography = secondhand because it covers a life (challenge tags 'about' and 'neither'), the secondhand account is always more correct or the firsthand one always truer (step 4 prediction 'the history book: it has the facts', challenge tags 'trust' and 'trust2', mastery m7), and a sentence is firsthand just because it has facts or secondhand just because it has dates (challenge tag 'big'). The step 5 rewrite targets keeping I/we and feelings in a third-person account.

lab_distinct.evidence: flagacct is built on comparing two accounts of one event: a was-the-writer-there source sort into a notebook and a book, a line sort between a child's diary and a history book of the same flood, a two-circle Venn diagram with diary-only, both and book-only drop regions, a which-account-answers-this question picker with a Neither option, and a rewrite step that turns diary lines into a neutral third-person voice. No other flagship lab has a Venn drop zone or a voice rewrite; lab_distinct passed under 30% against every flagship lab, including flagpov and flagteller.

lab_teaches.evidence: The child meets each idea through feedback before the step summary states it: a biography dropped on firsthand returns 'The writer was not there. They put it together from other people's words and records: secondhand'; '£5 million cost' dropped in diary-only returns 'A girl of 10 that night could not know this. It was counted or decided later: book only'; 'What did the mayor eat for breakfast?' answered Diary returns 'Neither account was there for that or could know it'. The step summaries ('The diary zooms in on one girl. The book zooms out to the whole town.') come only after every item is placed.

predictions.evidence: Two predictions each hold a tempting wrong option that the lab then disproves: 'firsthand: it is all about her' for a biography (the sort files the biography under secondhand with the reason) and 'the history book: it has the facts' for which account is more useful (the question step sends feelings, sounds and Mia's cat questions to the diary and two questions to Neither). The completion line names the learner's own pick.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Five challenge questions, every wrong option tagged with its own message: 'book' (a science book was written later), 'bio' (about a person but written by someone else), 'about' (being about a person does not make it secondhand), 'neither' (an autobiography is a true life story), 'feel' (an astronaut could not count TV viewers; numbers come from records), 'same' (they do not say the same things), 'big' (a checked fact in calm words is not an eyewitness line), 'trust' and 'trust2' (each kind can miss things; compare both).

readability.evidence: Measured with learn/readability.py: kid FK grade 3.8 (family limit 5.0) and adult 7.0 (limit 10.0) after the first adult draft scored 10.7 and was rewritten in shorter sentences. Kid text defines firsthand and secondhand with one test (was the writer there?) and three everyday examples each; biography is explained in the sentence where it appears.

no_filler.evidence: Every kid sentence gives a definition, an example or a use; the adult text gives the US and England requirements, the one-question test and three lenses (focus, facts, words), four named mistakes and what the lab does. The content gate found no filler phrases and the explanation is under 12% the same as every other lesson.

mobile.evidence: Checked 360 px Android screenshots in light and dark for all six steps. The first Venn screenshot clipped both circles at the edges and showed a white 'Both' label on a light overlap in dark mode; the radius and gap were reduced so both circles fit, and the overlap is now filled green with dark green text. The sort headers now wrap onto two lines (Firsthand / I was there) instead of shrinking, answer cards are 74 px tall in one row, and rewrite options are full-width 58 px buttons. The browser walkthrough passed on iPhone 13.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas action has a button under the canvas: the two bins with the current source in each aria-label, 'Diary only', 'Both' and 'Book only' for the Venn with the detail named, the three accounts for each question, and 'History book: …' for each rewrite. Tapping a bin, a Venn region or a card also works, and cards can be dragged. The canvas aria-label is rewritten after every action, challenge feedback is a role=status live region, and axe (WCAG 2.1 AA) found no violations in either theme on desktop and iPhone 13.

sources: Common Core State Standards for English Language Arts, Reading: Informational Text RI.4.6
Department for Education (2013) The national curriculum in England: English programme of study, Years 5 and 6 reading comprehension
